column3: Four medial M structures are the motor pathway, medial lemniscus, MLF and motor cranial-nerve nuclei/fascicles; four lateral S structures are spinocerebellar, spinothalamic, sensory trigeminal and sympathetic pathways.
column4: Medial lesions favour contralateral weakness/proprioceptive loss with ipsilateral motor cranial-nerve or gaze findings; lateral lesions favour ipsilateral ataxia/Horner/facial pain-temperature loss with contralateral body pain-temperature loss.
column5: The Rule of 4s is a localisation framework, not a list of named vascular syndromes; first identify level and side, then decide medial versus lateral.
column6: Given a combination of cranial-nerve and long-tract signs, identify the brainstem level, lesion side and medial/lateral position.

column3: CN III-IV arise from the midbrain, V-VIII from the pons and IX-XII from the medulla; clinically these nuclei/fascicles provide a rapid level marker.
column4: An ipsilateral ocular, facial or bulbar cranial-nerve deficit can identify both the brainstem level and usually the side of the lesion.
column5: Do not simply allocate CN I-IV to midbrain: I and II are not brainstem nerves; the clinically useful midbrain localisers are III and IV.
column6: Use the affected cranial nerve first: III/IV → midbrain, V-VIII → pons, IX-XII → medulla.

column3: Medial structures include corticospinal motor fibres, medial lemniscus, MLF and the relevant medial motor cranial-nerve structures.
column4: A medial lesion may give an ipsilateral motor cranial-nerve deficit plus contralateral weakness and/or contralateral vibration-proprioception loss; MLF involvement adds conjugate-gaze dysfunction.
column5: Contralateral pain-temperature loss with ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss instead points toward lateral brainstem structures.
column6: An ipsilateral VI palsy with contralateral hemiparesis should immediately suggest a medial pontine lesion.

column3: Lateral structures include spinocerebellar pathways, spinothalamic tract, spinal trigeminal sensory pathway and descending sympathetic fibres.
column4: Typical findings are ipsilateral ataxia, ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and contralateral body pain-temperature loss.
column5: Marked corticospinal weakness is less characteristic of a purely lateral lesion; crossed pain-temperature loss is particularly valuable.
column6: Use ipsilateral face plus contralateral body pain-temperature loss to recognise a lateral brainstem lesion and then use cranial-nerve/bulbar signs to determine pons versus medulla.

column3: Corticospinal fibres descend through cerebral peduncle, ventral pons and medullary pyramids before most cross at the caudal medullary pyramidal decussation.
column4: A unilateral lesion above the pyramidal decussation causes contralateral UMN limb weakness.
column5: Below the decussation, spinal-cord corticospinal lesions cause ipsilateral weakness; do not apply the brainstem laterality rule below the crossing.
column6: Right brainstem corticospinal involvement explains left-sided pyramidal weakness.

column3: Dorsal-column fibres synapse in gracile/cuneate nuclei and cross in the caudal medulla before ascending as the medial lemniscus.
column4: Brainstem medial-lemniscus injury causes contralateral loss of vibration, proprioception and discriminative touch.
column5: Pain-temperature loss is spinothalamic, not medial lemniscal; distinguish sensory modality before localising.
column6: Contralateral loss of joint position/vibration accompanying a motor cranial-nerve palsy supports a medial brainstem lesion.

column3: Body pain-temperature fibres cross near their spinal level of entry and ascend contralaterally in the anterolateral/spinothalamic pathway.
column4: A unilateral brainstem lesion therefore causes contralateral body pain-temperature loss.
column5: The face uses trigeminal pathways; opposite-sided face and body pain-temperature deficits are not contradictory but strongly localising.
column6: Left body pain-temperature loss with right facial pain-temperature loss points to a right lateral brainstem lesion.

column3: Facial pain-temperature fibres descend ipsilaterally in the spinal trigeminal tract before synapsing in the spinal trigeminal nucleus.
column4: Lateral brainstem injury causes ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss, often with contralateral body pain-temperature loss from spinothalamic involvement.
column5: Do not expect face and body pain-temperature loss to be on the same side in the classic crossed lateral brainstem pattern.
column6: Right facial pain-temperature loss plus left body pain-temperature loss localises to the right lateral brainstem.

column3: The MLF links the abducens nucleus of one side to the contralateral oculomotor medial-rectus subnucleus, coordinating conjugate horizontal gaze.
column4: A unilateral MLF lesion produces impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye during horizontal gaze with contralateral abducting nystagmus.
column5: An MLF lesion is an internuclear gaze disorder, not an isolated CN III palsy; ptosis and pupillary abnormalities are not expected from an isolated MLF lesion.
column6: Failure of the left eye to adduct on right gaze with right abducting nystagmus localises to the left MLF.

column3: INO results from interruption of the MLF between the abducens and contralateral oculomotor nuclei.
column4: The eye ipsilateral to the lesion fails to adduct during horizontal gaze; the abducting contralateral eye often develops nystagmus, while convergence may be preserved.
column5: Bilateral INO in a younger adult strongly suggests demyelination; a unilateral acute INO in an older adult may represent brainstem ischaemia.
column6: Left adduction failure during right gaze with preserved primary-position ocular motor function should prompt localisation to the left MLF rather than peripheral CN III.

column1: Horizontal gaze centre: PPRF and abducens nucleus
column3: The pontine paramedian reticular formation drives ipsilateral horizontal gaze via the abducens nucleus, which simultaneously activates ipsilateral lateral rectus and contralateral medial rectus through the MLF.
column4: A destructive PPRF or abducens-nucleus lesion causes inability of both eyes to gaze toward the side of the pontine lesion.
column5: This differs from an isolated CN VI fascicle/nerve lesion, where only the ipsilateral eye cannot abduct.
column6: If neither eye can look left, localise to the left PPRF/abducens nucleus rather than the left abducens nerve alone.

column3: A dorsal pontine lesion involving the ipsilateral PPRF/abducens nucleus plus the ipsilateral MLF combines an ipsilateral horizontal-gaze palsy with an INO.
column4: The ipsilateral eye has essentially no horizontal movement; the contralateral eye can only abduct, usually with abducting nystagmus.
column5: An isolated INO preserves conjugate gaze toward the opposite side; one-and-a-half syndrome adds an ipsilateral conjugate-gaze palsy.
column6: Use the combination of gaze palsy and INO to localise a compact lesion in the ipsilateral dorsal pons.

column3: The midbrain contains CN III/IV structures, cerebral peduncles, MLF and cerebellar/red-nucleus pathways.
column4: An ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral pyramidal weakness is a classic crossed midbrain pattern; additional tremor/ataxia depends on tegmental involvement.
column5: A peripheral CN III palsy alone does not prove a midbrain lesion; associated contralateral long-tract signs are the key localiser.
column6: Left down-and-out eye with ptosis plus right hemiparesis localises to the left midbrain.

column3: A ventral midbrain lesion damages the ipsilateral oculomotor fascicle and adjacent cerebral-peduncle corticospinal/corticobulbar fibres.
column4: Ipsilateral CN III palsy occurs with contralateral hemiparesis, often including lower facial weakness.
column5: Do not confuse with an isolated compressive III palsy: contralateral pyramidal signs indicate a midbrain fascicular lesion.
column6: Right III palsy plus left UMN weakness localises to the right ventral midbrain.

column3: The pons contains CN V-VIII nuclei/fascicles plus corticospinal, sensory, gaze and cerebellar connections.
column4: Ipsilateral VI/VII or horizontal-gaze findings accompanied by contralateral body motor/sensory deficits strongly localise to the pons.
column5: LMN facial weakness with opposite-sided limb signs is pontine; cortical facial weakness is contralateral and usually forehead-sparing.
column6: Left LMN facial weakness plus right hemiparesis localises to the left pons.

column3: Paramedian pontine injury can involve corticospinal fibres, medial lemniscus and abducens fascicle/nucleus or nearby gaze pathways.
column4: Typical pattern is ipsilateral VI/gaze abnormality with contralateral weakness, with possible contralateral vibration-proprioception loss.
column5: Lateral pontine/AICA lesions instead emphasise facial paralysis, hearing/vestibular symptoms, ataxia and crossed pain-temperature loss.
column6: Right VI palsy plus left hemiparesis and left vibration loss points to the right medial pons.

column3: The medulla contains CN IX-XII structures, pyramids, medial lemniscus, nucleus ambiguus, vestibular/cerebellar and lateral sensory pathways.
column4: Dysphagia/hoarseness suggests nucleus ambiguus/lateral medulla; ipsilateral XII weakness with contralateral pyramidal and proprioceptive deficits suggests medial medulla.
column5: Use bulbar pattern to separate lateral medullary disease from pontine ocular/facial syndromes.
column6: First decide whether the key localiser is IX/X bulbar dysfunction or XII tongue weakness, then apply crossed body findings.

column3: A medial medullary lesion affects the pyramid, medial lemniscus and ipsilateral hypoglossal fascicle.
column4: It causes contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral vibration-proprioception loss and ipsilateral tongue weakness; the protruded tongue deviates toward the lesion.
column5: Lateral medullary syndrome instead causes nucleus-ambiguus dysfunction, ataxia, Horner syndrome and crossed pain-temperature loss without the classic pyramidal triad.
column6: Tongue deviating left with right hemiparesis and right proprioceptive loss localises to the left medial medulla.

column3: CN III supplies levator palpebrae, most extraocular muscles and parasympathetic pupillary fibres; a fascicular lesion may accompany nearby midbrain long-tract damage.
column4: Palsy produces ptosis and a down-and-out eye, with possible mydriasis; contralateral weakness implies an ipsilateral midbrain lesion.
column5: An acute painful pupil-involving isolated III palsy raises concern for external compression such as posterior communicating artery aneurysm rather than automatically implying intrinsic midbrain stroke.
column6: Down-and-out left eye plus right UMN weakness = left midbrain; isolated painful left III palsy with mydriasis requires urgent compressive-aneurysm assessment.

column3: Trochlear fibres arise from the dorsal midbrain and uniquely decussate before exiting; the nerve supplies superior oblique.
column4: Palsy causes vertical/torsional diplopia, typically worse looking down such as when reading or descending stairs.
column5: A trochlear nuclear lesion affects the contralateral superior oblique, whereas a fascicular or peripheral nerve lesion affects the ipsilateral eye.
column6: Use the unusual IV decussation when a dorsal-midbrain lesion and the affected eye appear to be on opposite sides.

column3: CN VI arises in the pons and supplies lateral rectus; its nucleus also participates in conjugate horizontal gaze.
column4: An isolated fascicular/peripheral VI lesion causes failure of ipsilateral abduction; an abducens-nucleus lesion causes ipsilateral conjugate-gaze palsy.
column5: A VI palsy may also occur as a false-localising sign in raised intracranial pressure because of the nerve's long intracranial course.
column6: Right eye cannot abduct plus left hemiparesis strongly suggests right pontine fascicular involvement; inability of both eyes to gaze right suggests the right abducens nucleus/PPRF.

column3: Supranuclear corticobulbar input to the upper facial nucleus is bilateral, while lower facial muscles receive predominantly contralateral cortical input; the facial nucleus/fascicle itself supplies the ipsilateral whole face.
column4: A cerebral UMN lesion causes contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing; pontine nuclear/fascicular or peripheral VII lesions cause ipsilateral whole-face LMN weakness.
column5: Forehead sparing is useful but not infallible; interpret it with the rest of the neurological examination.
column6: Left whole-face weakness plus right limb weakness localises to the left pons; left lower-face weakness plus left limb weakness suggests a right supranuclear lesion.

column3: Nucleus ambiguus in the lateral medulla provides branchial motor output principally through IX/X to pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles.
column4: Lesion causes dysphagia, hoarseness, impaired palatal elevation and reduced gag motor response, classically in lateral medullary syndrome.
column5: Prominent dysphagia/hoarseness distinguishes lateral medulla/PICA from classic lateral pons/AICA, where facial paralysis and hearing symptoms are more characteristic.
column6: Acute vertigo plus hoarseness, ipsilateral ataxia and crossed pain-temperature loss should localise to the lateral medulla.

column3: A lower motor neuron hypoglossal lesion weakens the ipsilateral tongue; on protrusion the tongue deviates toward the weak side.
column4: A medullary XII fascicular lesion combined with contralateral hemiparesis is a classic medial medullary crossed pattern.
column5: UMN corticobulbar tongue weakness is subtler and deviation is away from the cortical lesion; do not use the LMN rule indiscriminately.
column6: Tongue deviates right with left hemiparesis = right medial medulla.

column1: Cerebral hemisphere versus pontine gaze deviation
column3: The frontal eye field drives gaze to the opposite side through contralateral pontine gaze centres; destructive hemispheric and pontine lesions therefore produce different gaze patterns.
column4: A large destructive cerebral hemispheric lesion may produce gaze preference toward the cortical lesion, whereas a destructive pontine horizontal-gaze-centre lesion prevents gaze toward the pontine lesion.
column5: Do not interpret eye deviation without checking whether the abnormality is a gaze preference, conjugate-gaze palsy, isolated ocular-motor palsy or INO.
column6: Use gaze direction together with hemiparesis and cranial-nerve findings to distinguish a large hemispheric stroke from a pontine lesion.
